standard.title: Seek, Give or Deny Permission
standard.description: explore how to seek, give or deny permission respectfully when sharing possessions or personal space
standard.prior_knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students have informal experience of asking and being asked to share. No prior structured curriculum exploration of consent, rights and respectful negotiation.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore and practise how to seek, give or deny permission respectfully when sharing possessions or personal space, recognising their right to say no.

nodes.label: The importance of asking permission
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why asking for permission matters when sharing possessions or personal space, and identify situations where permission is needed.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one situation where they would need to ask permission before sharing or accessing something, and give a reason why asking is important.
nodes.typical_width: Explore multiple situations requiring permission — sharing possessions, personal space, and activity roles; explain why asking matters for respect and rights; recognise the right to say no as part of respecting others.
wider: Explore permission and consent in play contexts across different cultural settings, including First Nations Australian negotiation practices in games
Discuss digital contexts where permission is needed — e.g. taking or sharing a photo of someone
Connect body autonomy to permission — explaining that our bodies belong to us and others must ask before touching
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding why permission matters, practising how to ask becomes mechanical compliance. The Y1-2 equivalent (practising strategies) requires this conceptual foundation. Body autonomy connections are foundational to protective behaviours work in AC9HPFP05.

response_modes.reason: The concept of rights — including the right to say no — requires explicit, teacher-led discussion. Scenario-based exploration (what would you do if... ?) is more effective than rule-telling.
Permission situations vary: possessions, personal space, digital contexts, bodily autonomy. Varied context discussion prevents students from associating permission only with object-sharing.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Body autonomy and digital consent contexts extend permission understanding well beyond object-sharing and connect to the protective behaviours standard, providing rich cross-standard learning.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one situation where asking permission is required
Gives a simple reason why asking permission is important for respecting others

nodes.label: Practising seeking, giving and denying permission
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can practise and refine how to ask for permission and how to give or deny permission respectfully, including respecting someone's right to say no.
nodes.minimum_width: Practise asking permission in at least one play or sharing context using respectful language, and demonstrate accepting a yes or no response.
nodes.typical_width: Practise and refine seeking, giving and denying permission across play and imaginative situations; demonstrate respect for different responses including 'no'; negotiate roles through imaginative and shared play while maintaining awareness of rights.
wider: Practise permission-seeking in physical activity contexts involving personal space (e.g. partner games, dance, contact activities)
Use role-play to rehearse scenarios where permission is denied and explore how to respond respectfully
Discuss and practise digital scenarios involving permission (e.g. asking before taking a photo)

response_modes.reason: Permission-seeking and denial is a practised social skill. Foundation students need repeated, structured role-play and play experiences before respectful language and acceptance of 'no' become habitual.

success_criteria: Uses respectful language or gesture to ask permission in a play or sharing context
Accepts a yes or no response to a permission request without acting disrespectfully
